Tropic Ridge Wind Farm - Integrated Cost and Schedule Risk Analysis¶

Ridgeline: cost and schedule risk for capital projects, from bid to handover. A CBL Analytics product.

Tropic Ridge Wind Farm is a synthetic project. Its register, schedule and every figure in this report were generated to demonstrate the method; they describe no real project.

Executive summary¶

Schedule risk analysis on the Stage 3 CPM replay indicates a mean schedule slip of 42.7 days, equivalent to $3.97M at $35,000 per working day. The Stage 2.5 Mode-scenario comparators span 32.1 to 42.7 days mean; they are shown for continuity with earlier reporting and are not the headline.

The headline is one Stage 3 distribution: each risk's delay is injected at its declared gating activity and propagated through the programme's own logic, and the P50 to P95 spread is project uncertainty rather than a spread between Mode assumptions. The table below is the Stage 2.5 comparator range - the DP Review baseline and the All Series upper bound that earlier reports published as the headline - with the Stage 3 figure placed between them for reconciliation. Cost analysis is independent of Mode classification.

Scenario Mean schedule slip (days) Mean cost ($M) P80 contingency ($M) Notes
DP Review baseline (Mode as registered) 32.06 3.98 7.00 Conservative starting point
Stage 3 (CPM replay, one distribution) 42.68 3.97 7.48
All Series (all-Series upper bound) 42.65 3.98 7.48 Methodological extreme

Distribution¶

These charts show the full probability distribution of schedule slip, not just point estimates. The S-curve shows cumulative probability; the histogram shows the right-skewed shape. Cumulative probability runs from 0 (no slip) to 100 (all simulated outcomes are at or below this level). Reference percentiles (P50, P80, P90, P95) are marked as vertical lines.

The right-skew is a direct consequence of low-probability, high-impact risks. Mean is pulled to the right of median by the tail; the distance between P80 and P95 widens as Mode shifts from Parallel toward Series. Selecting a contingency at the mean leaves roughly half the simulated outcomes uncovered; selecting at P80 covers four in five. The choice is risk appetite, not arithmetic.

Decomposition of integrated P80 contingency: cost-P80 plus schedule-P80 dollarised at the day rate ($35,000/wd), less the diversification adjustment from joint sampling, equals the integrated P80 reported in the headline.

Schedule drivers¶

The schedule tornado ranks risks by probability-weighted mean contribution in days, not by P80. For low-probability discrete risks the P80 quantile is mathematically zero; reporting at P80 would obscure the contribution. Probability-weighted mean (firing probability times mean impact when fired) is the appropriate ranking metric and matches the EMV first-principles calculation.

Schedule slip concentrates by Risk Breakdown Structure (RBS) category as well as by individual risk. The 12-scenario counterfactual table quantifies how the headline mean schedule slip would shift under each plausible single-risk Mode reclassification. Each row shows mean slip if that risk were reclassified to Series while all other classifications remain at DP Review. Rows with delta > 1 day from baseline are the high-leverage Mode decisions; resolving these classifications narrows the headline range substantially.

PM review should prioritise the rows highlighted above. The highest-leverage classifications are the ones where reclassifying to Series shifts the mean by more than one day; these are the decisions that move the contingency. Risks whose Mode shift produces sub-day movement contribute to range width but not to the central estimate.

Two risk matrices compared side by side. Left: traditional probability vs mean impact (days when fired), the matrix engineers see in standard QRA. Mean impact when fired is the PERT mean of the register Optimistic/Most Likely/Pessimistic days and is independent of Mode classification. Right: probability vs probability-weighted impact (probability times Mode-multiplied mean impact), the matrix that ranks risks the way Monte Carlo does. Markers on the right panel reflect the Stage 3 Mode scenario; the schedule-drivers table immediately above uses the same scenario for consistency, so right-panel x-coordinates match the table's Probability x mean impact column. Each marker is a risk; the top contributors are labelled with their risk IDs.

Compare the position of low-probability, high-impact risks across the two panels. On the traditional matrix they sit at low probability and high mean impact - easy to deprioritise in standard prioritisation. On the probability-weighted matrix they rank higher because the integrated mean impact captures the tail. This differential ranking is the visual case for MC over standard matrices.

Reconciliation¶

How does this MC result compare to first-principles and gut-feel methods that the reader is likely familiar with? The table below lists six approaches that all aim at the same question - how much contingency? - and shows what each one produces against the same risk register.

Approach Schedule contingency (days) Cost contingency ($M) Notes
Engineering judgement (10% of programme) 45.00 NaN Common rule of thumb
Engineering judgement (20% of programme) 90.00 NaN Conservative gut-feel
Sum of pessimistic impacts (worst case, no probability) 213.00 25.22 Adds all worst-case impacts; ignores probability
EMV (sum of probability x ML impact) 38.45 3.26 First-principles probability-weighted estimate (deterministic)
MC mean, Stage 3 headline (recommended central estimate) 42.68 3.97 Reconciles with EMV; adds tail visibility
MC P80, Stage 3 headline 60.99 5.42 Useful for contingency floor
MC P95, Stage 3 headline 79.88 7.32 For risk-aware contingency

MC mean reconciles with EMV (sum of probability times mean impact) to within MC noise - this is a validation check that the simulation is implementing the underlying first-principles calculation correctly. Beyond that reconciliation, MC adds tail visibility (P80, P95) that deterministic methods cannot provide. Engineering judgement bounds (10-20% of programme) bracket the MC result, confirming the result sits within the range a seasoned engineer would recognise.

How is the integrated cost-plus-schedule P80 constructed? The waterfall below traces the components: cost-only P80, then schedule slip dollarised, then the diversification adjustment (or anti-diversification) under joint sampling. The two scenarios shown are the headline and the All Series upper bound.

Under the headline distribution, integrated P80 may exceed the naive sum of cost-only P80 and schedule-only P80. This is a counterintuitive but real result of joint sampling: when a low-probability, high-impact tail risk couples cost and schedule simultaneously, the joint P80 captures correlated worst-case behaviour the marginal P80s miss. Under All Series, joint sampling produces a small diversification benefit because cost-driver and schedule-driver risks fire independently.

Recommendations

  • Prioritise risk-treatment plans for the top schedule drivers: WT-008, WT-001, WT-021. Resolution of these risks narrows the headline contingency materially.
  • Treatment effort focused on WT-008 ($0.66M P80 contribution) reduces cost contingency more than effort spread across the long tail.
  • Use the per-risk diagnostic outputs (audit trail appendix) to drive targeted risk treatment plans for the top-3 cost and schedule drivers.

Methodology and caveats¶

  • Joint sampling mechanism. The integrated Monte Carlo engine shares a single severity uniform per dual-coded risk per iteration, driving both the cost dispatch and the schedule PERT draw. This produces correlated cost and schedule severities for the 10 risks flagged as time-impacting in the project risk register. Cost-only risks use independent severity uniforms. The mechanism preserves marginal calibration with the standalone cost and schedule engines while enabling diversification benefit measurement at the joint percentile.
  • Schedule classifications. Series, Hybrid, and Parallel classifications for the dual-coded risks reflect the conservative starting-point informed by current schedule structure. Sensitivity of the headline to classification choice is bounded and documented in the appendices.
  • Full-network CPM replay. The schedule analysis replays the programme's full activity network on every iteration: each activity's duration is sampled, a forward and backward pass is run over the whole network, and the finish date is read from that pass. The critical path is therefore an output of each iteration rather than a subset fixed in advance, and an activity off the planned critical path contributes to finish-date slip whenever sampling puts it on the path. The deterministic critical path quoted in the appendices is the activity set with zero float under a single zero-risk pass; where chains tie on float, that set is a superset of any one longest path. Series, Hybrid and Parallel classifications are carried from the strawman and reported for context; under the full-network replay they do not multiply a risk's impact, because the network decides how a delay propagates.

Distribution choice per risk reflects the shape of the underlying uncertainty:

  • PERT (default), three-point Optimistic / Most Likely / Pessimistic where the Most Likely value carries more weight than the extremes; the standard for contingency analysis.
  • Triangular, three-point with no central-tendency weighting; used where the Most Likely value is genuinely uncertain.
  • Lognormal, right-skewed continuous; used for cost categories with fat-tail exposure (e.g. commodity price spikes).
  • Binary, fires fully or not at all; used for irreducible step-change events.

The methodology aligns with the following standards and recommended practices: AACE RP 44R-08 Risk Analysis and Contingency Determination Using Range Estimating; AACE RP 65R-11 Integrated Cost and Schedule Risk Analysis Using Risk Drivers and Monte Carlo Simulation of a CPM Model; AACE RP 57R-09 Integrated Cost and Schedule Risk Analysis Using Monte Carlo Simulation of a CPM Model (cited as future scope for full CPM-based replay); AACE RP 113R-21 Integrated Cost and Schedule Risk Analysis - Sampling and Computational Aspects; PMI PMBOK 7th edition (Project Risk Management); ISO 31000:2018 (Risk management guidelines).

Convergence diagnostic: 95% bootstrap CI on the integrated P80 cost across iteration counts 1k → 100k. Band tightens as iterations grow; convergence is reached when further iterations no longer materially shift the band.

Monte Carlo simulation produces a sample, not the truth. The convergence diagnostic above shows how the headline figure stabilises as iteration count grows; a tight 95% bootstrap confidence band at the iteration count this run used indicates the simulation has run enough iterations for the headline to be reliable to within the band's width. The diagnostic measures Monte Carlo error only, it does not measure model uncertainty in the inputs (probability estimates, three-point distributions, Mode classifications) or in the methodology itself.

  • The cost Monte Carlo engine groups risks by their underlying driver, common conditions that increase the joint probability of multiple risks firing together. A tight construction market that drives commodity prices up simultaneously raises the probability of multiple downstream risks; modelling those as independent would understate the joint tail exposure at exactly the contingency-relevant probability levels. Risks within a Correlation Group fire together more often than chance per the coefficient shown; risks across groups fire independently.
  • The table below maps each active Correlation Group to its driver description, the member risks, and the joint-firing coefficient. Together with the per-risk Probability and three-point distributions in the register, the CG mapping is the third leg of the cost MC's correlation structure, the other two being within-CG joint sampling (Cholesky-decomposed correlated uniforms) and the shared severity uniform on the dual-coded risks for joint cost-and-schedule sampling.

Limitations of current analysis

  • Per-party views are deferred to the next stage. The current deliverable presents the whole-project view only.
  • Criticality assessment uses the conservative starting-point classification informed by current schedule structure
  • Per-activity attribution of the finish to individual risks is deferred. The replay reports the project finish and each activity's criticality; the per-risk driver ranking beside it is the additive comparator basis, not the replay.
  • Sensitivity analysis on individual risk probabilities and impacts (one-at-a-time, top-driver) is deferred to the next stage.
  • This deliverable presents the event-risk contingency (Layer 2) on an input base estimate. Systemic uncertainty on that base (Layer 1) is outside its view: where a register enables Layer 1, the Tier 1 owner view samples it and reports the distribution of base plus contingency as a product output.

None of these are limitations of the methodology; they are inputs not yet available or capabilities deferred to the next stage. When inputs land, the analysis extends without re-engineering.

Appendices¶

Mode-classification sensitivity¶

Methodology¶

Caveats

  • The headline is a single Stage 3 distribution. Mode classifications play no part in it; they remain visible only in the Stage 2.5 comparator range beside the reconciliation.
  • Schedule analysis operates on the full programme logic exported from the planning tool. Delays propagate along that logic; a gating activity outside a risk's cohort is refused before any iteration runs.
  • Liquidated damages and IDC layers are deferred to a later stage pending commercial input confirmation.

References

  • AACE 57R-09: Risk analysis and contingency determination using expected value (cost engine basis).
  • AACE 65R-11: Integrated cost and schedule risk analysis using Monte Carlo simulation.
  • PMI Practice Standard for Project Risk Management.

PERT distributions for cost and schedule severity per risk (opt/ml/pess from the project risk register). Lognormal available for selected event risks where right-tail behaviour matters. Bernoulli gates for risk firing. Cholesky-decomposed correlated uniforms for within-CG correlation.

Disclaimer¶

  • Joint sampling mechanism. The integrated Monte Carlo engine shares a single severity uniform per dual-coded risk per iteration, driving both the cost dispatch and the schedule PERT draw. This produces correlated cost and schedule severities for the 10 risks flagged as time-impacting in the project risk register. Cost-only risks use independent severity uniforms. The mechanism preserves marginal calibration with the standalone cost and schedule engines while enabling diversification benefit measurement at the joint percentile.
  • Schedule classifications. Series, Hybrid, and Parallel classifications for the dual-coded risks reflect the conservative starting-point informed by current schedule structure. Sensitivity of the headline to classification choice is bounded and documented in the appendices.
  • Full-network CPM replay. The schedule analysis replays the programme's full activity network on every iteration: each activity's duration is sampled, a forward and backward pass is run over the whole network, and the finish date is read from that pass. The critical path is therefore an output of each iteration rather than a subset fixed in advance, and an activity off the planned critical path contributes to finish-date slip whenever sampling puts it on the path. The deterministic critical path quoted in the appendices is the activity set with zero float under a single zero-risk pass; where chains tie on float, that set is a superset of any one longest path. Series, Hybrid and Parallel classifications are carried from the strawman and reported for context; under the full-network replay they do not multiply a risk's impact, because the network decides how a delay propagates.
  • Multi-party views deferred. The current deliverable presents the whole-project view only. EPC Contractor, Wind Farm Owner, and Shared stakeholder views are deferred to a later stage pending confirmation of the risk-share parameters and counterparty allocation rules.
  • Day-rate basis. The day rate used to dollarise schedule slip is sourced from the Risk Register Variables sheet via the strawman methodology workbook. The same value is used by the standalone schedule engine, the integrated engine, and the executive summary so all reported dollar conversions are consistent.

Its version date appears in the audit trail appendix. When the strawman is reissued, this deliverable re-runs against the amended state and supersedes the prior version.
  • Engine versioning. The cost Monte Carlo engine, schedule MC engine, integrated cost+schedule engine, and final composition layer carry version stamps recorded in the audit trail appendix. The run date and seed are recorded so the deliverable is reproducible from the strawman snapshot it was generated against.
